Guided Inquiry

1 · The apparatus

Here’s the apparatus. A particle source emits particles with a random magnetic moment μ, and the beam passes through an inhomogeneous magnetic field aligned along the z-axis, as you can see. The force on each particle is proportional to the projection of the magnetic moment along z, which we’ll call μz. Quantum mechanically, the magnetic moment is proportional to the particle’s spin.

2 · The classical prediction

Let’s start with the classical picture. Classically, what do you think the distribution of particles on the detector screen would be?

3 · The split

Here’s the quantum version. The source now emits spin j = 1/2 particles, and the beam splits in two. Why do you think that happens?

4 · Counting the bands

Let’s push that further. For particles of spin j, how many bands do you think the beam splits into? The spin j is yours to change — try a few values and let the detector decide.

5 · Doubling the gradient

One last experiment. We’ll double the field gradient while the source emits j = 1/2 particles. How do you think the force on each particle changes?

The Physics

Stern–Gerlach experiment · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The sim sends neutral atoms through a magnet whose field changes with height, and records where each atom lands on a screen. The pattern shows which directions an atom's magnetic moment can take, which is how this experiment first tested whether those directions are quantised.

What you'll learn

  • Why a magnet whose field varies in space can push an atom that has no charge.
  • What the screen shows if the moment may point any way, and if only some directions are allowed.
  • How the spin j and the field gradient each change the pattern.
  • How to read the counts on the screen as probabilities.
The set-up. The pointed N pole makes the field stronger near the top of the gap.

What's on screen

  • Atoms (green) leave the source. Inside the magnet each takes the colour of its Beam Legend row.
  • Magnet: N pole above (pointed), S pole below. |B| max and |B| min mark the strongest and weakest field.
  • Detection window: each atom that reaches the screen leaves a dot. Its title names the rule running.
  • Orange dots: the classical prediction (section 04).
  • Sidebar: the Total detected, and the Beam Legend with a count per row.
See itStart the beam from the opening settings. Watch for: green atoms changing colour as they enter the magnet, and the Total counter rising.

03

A field gradient pushes a neutral atom

The atoms carry no net charge, so the magnetic field exerts no Lorentz force on them. They do carry a magnetic moment μ, locked to their angular momentum J:

The z component of μ is set by mJ, one of the allowed values of Jz/ħ.

In a uniform field the energy U = −μ·B only twists the moment and gives no net force. A force needs the field to change with position, which is why one pole is pointed:

The force along z is the z component of μ times the gradient.

In the sim ∂B/∂z is positive, so an atom with positive mJ is pushed down and one with negative mJ up. The push acts only while the atom is between the poles. After that it drifts in a straight line to the screen.

See itRun the opening settings and follow the colours. Watch for: pink atoms bending down inside the magnet and blue atoms bending up.
04

Classical physics predicts a continuous smear

Suppose the moment could point in any direction with equal chance. Then μz would take every value from −μ to +μ with equal weight, and so would the force. The same 1/(2μ) applies everywhere between the two edges, so the screen would fill evenly.

p is a probability density: the chance that μz lies in a small interval dμz is p dμz. Left: classical. Right: quantum.

In the sim, the classical mode gives each atom a random value anywhere between −j and +j, so its edges sit where the outermost quantum values would land. The orange dots then fill the space between with no gap.

See itRun the classical rule at j = 2. Watch for: orange dots filling the screen evenly between two edges, with no empty gaps.
05

The projection takes only 2j + 1 values

Quantum theory allows Jz only the values mJħ, with mJ = −j, −j + 1, …, +j. That is 2j + 1 values in steps of one. Each value gives its own force, so each gives its own place on the screen.

The sim's five settings of j at 3 T/m, with the sim's colours. Spacing is the same in every column.
  • Integer j includes mJ = 0, so one band sits on the centre line. Half-integer j does not.
  • j = 0 allows only mJ = 0. Then μz = 0 and there is no force at any gradient.
  • A larger j adds bands outward without moving the ones already there.
See itSet j = 2 at 3 T/m. Watch for: five separate groups of dots, one on the centre line, with a gap between neighbours.
06

The gradient sets the spacing

An atom is pushed for the time L/v it spends in the magnet, then drifts a distance D. Adding the two stages gives its height on the screen:

L is the magnet length, D the drift, v the atom's speed, ζ the gap between neighbouring bands.
j ∂B/∂z

These sliders move the sim too. Changing j clears the screen.

  • Linear. ζ is proportional to ∂B/∂z, so doubling the gradient doubles every gap. It is not squared.
  • Equal gaps. Band positions are −mJζ, so neighbours are always ζ apart.
  • Slower atoms bend more. ζ goes as 1/v², so the sim's small spread of speeds blurs each band a little.
See itRun 3 T/m, then 6 T/m, each for a few seconds. Watch for: the gap between the bands about doubling.
07

An unpolarised beam fills each band equally

The magnet ties each atom's height to its mJ, so where an atom lands tells you which mJ it had. Quantum theory gives only the probability of each outcome:

cm are the amplitudes of the state entering the magnet.

The sim's source has no preferred direction, so every mJ has the same probability, 1/(2j + 1). After N atoms each band holds about N/(2j + 1), give or take √(Np(1 − p)). At j = 1/2 and N = 100 that is 50 ± 5: close, but never forced to be equal.

The sim draws one mJ for each atom at the source and then moves the atom classically. That reproduces these counts. It cannot show an atom in a superposition, a precessing moment, or what a second magnet would do.

See itRun j = 1/2 at 20 atoms/s and watch the counts. Watch for: the pink and blue counts climbing together, rarely equal but never far apart.
08

Where it matters

  • The 1922 experiment. Stern and Gerlach sent silver atoms through a gradient of about 10 T/cm (1000 T/m) and found two bands where classical physics predicts one smear. The two bands are now explained by electron spin ½, proposed three years later.
  • Cold-atom experiments. Gradient pulses still separate atoms by spin state so that each state can be counted.
  • Beam experiments and clocks. Rabi's molecular-beam resonance method and caesium beam clocks use gradient magnets to select atoms in one state.
Go deeper: the size of the real split
Silver: gJ = 2, so μz = ∓μB.
  • The sim's 1–6 T/m is a teaching range, hundreds of times weaker than a real magnet, and its gJ = 1 halves the force. Only the ratios are physical.
09

Summary

In one line. A field gradient pushes each atom in proportion to mJ, so the screen shows 2j + 1 equally spaced bands whose gaps grow in proportion to ∂B/∂z.

Key points

  • The force is Fz = μz ∂B/∂z. No gradient, no force.
  • Classically μz takes every value. Quantum mechanics allows only mJ = −j … +j.
  • j sets how many bands there are. The gradient sets how far apart they are.
  • An unpolarised beam gives each band probability 1/(2j + 1).

Common mix-ups

  • "A stronger magnet splits the beam into more bands." The number of bands is fixed by j. The gradient only moves them apart.
  • "The classical pattern is just the quantum one, blurred." The classical rule has no gaps, and no gradient creates any.
  • "The field pushes the atoms because they are charged." The atoms are neutral. The force comes from the moment in a field gradient.

Things to try on your own

  • Set j = 0 and drag the gradient from 1 to 6 T/m. Describe the screen.
  • At j = 3/2, find which band sits closest to the centre line and note which mJ it is. Repeat at j = 1.
  • Run the classical rule at j = 1 and again at j = 2, and compare each pattern's edges with the outermost bands in quantum mode.
